title: The Binding of Ash and Bone

1.1 Opening – The Ordinary Evening.title: 1.1 - The Ordinary Evening
1.1 Opening – The Ordinary Evening.text:
The air in the village always smelled of woodsmoke and damp earth at this hour, when the last of the daylight slipped behind the western hills and the chimneys began to breathe.

Autumn had come early this year. It had crept down from the mountains in a succession of cold mornings, silvering the grass with frost and turning the woodland beyond the river to a riot of copper and gold. Now, near the end of the season, the leaves lay sodden beneath the hedgerows, and the bare branches scratched at the sky like the fingers of old men. Winter was coming. Everyone knew it. You could hear it in the way people spoke about their stores of flour, in the extra logs stacked beneath their eaves, in the hurried repairs to roofs that had survived another summer but might not survive the storms ahead.

Beyond the village, the fields stretched towards the darkening forest, where the trees grew so close together that even noon struggled to reach the ground. The oldest villagers claimed that the forest had once been smaller. That the trees had begun spreading after the gods died.

You had never believed them.

Or, more accurately, you had never found a reason to care.

There were more immediate things to concern yourself with than ancient stories. The roof above your head needed mending before the first heavy snow. Someone had left a broken cartwheel beside the well, where it had been gathering rainwater for three days. The baker had burned a batch of rye loaves that morning and spent the better part of an hour blaming everyone but himself. And the village bell, which had been losing its voice for as long as you could remember, had finally given up entirely that afternoon, leaving the hour to be announced by a small boy who could barely count to twelve.

Ordinary things. Irritating things. The sort of things that made a life.

You stood at the edge of the village green, watching the last of the day's work draw to a close.

A woman gathered washing from a line strung between two cottages. Somewhere behind you, a dog barked twice before being silenced by its owner. The blacksmith's hammer rang out one final time, then fell quiet. Through the open shutters of the alehouse came a burst of laughter, followed by the scrape of a chair across the floorboards.

Warm light spilled from windows, turning the muddy lanes amber. A little girl chased her brother around a stack of firewood, shrieking with laughter until their mother called them inside. The smell of onions frying in fat drifted from a nearby kitchen, rich enough to make your stomach tighten with hunger.

For a moment, you let yourself imagine that this was all there would ever be.

A small village. A cold winter. Familiar faces, familiar arguments, familiar roads leading nowhere particularly interesting. You would know which floorboards creaked in every house you entered. You would recognise the sound of every neighbour's footsteps. You would grow old hearing the same stories told by the same people, each version a little less accurate than the last.

Perhaps, you thought, there was something to be said for that.

The thought should have comforted you.

Instead, it settled somewhere beneath your ribs with the weight of a stone.

You had felt restless for weeks, although you could not have explained why. It was not unhappiness, exactly. There were people here you cared about, and places you would miss if you left. You knew the comfort of a familiar hearth and the quiet pleasure of walking a road without needing to look where you were going. You understood the rhythms of this place, the unspoken rules and small loyalties that held a community together.

But lately, the familiar had begun to feel like a garment that no longer fit.

You caught yourself staring towards the forest. You found yourself listening whenever strangers passed through the village, hungry for news of distant cities and unfamiliar lands. You wondered what lay beyond the mountains, beyond the borders marked on the old maps in the meeting house, beyond the places where the ink grew thin and the cartographers had simply written here be ruins.

Then you would feel foolish.

There were reasons people stayed in villages like yours. The roads were dangerous, the kingdoms quarrelsome, and the old magic—whatever remained of it—was something sensible people avoided. The world beyond your valley was not waiting to welcome you. It was a place where nobles bought favours with gold, witches sold secrets for blood, and men disappeared into the woods without leaving so much as a footprint.

That was what the travelling merchants said, at least.

They also claimed that the Fae had once ruled the continent.

You had heard the stories since childhood: beautiful, cruel creatures who could twist a promise into a chain and make a person's own name into a weapon. The old gods had supposedly given them dominion over the wild places, over the stars and the roots of mountains, over every living thing that drew breath beneath the moon.

Then came the war.

The gods died. The Fae vanished. Their palaces crumbled, their armies were scattered, and their magic passed into mortal bloodlines—or so the scholars argued, when they were not arguing about something else entirely.

Most people considered the whole business a convenient explanation for why the world was so thoroughly broken.

The village priest called the stories blasphemy. The old women called them warnings. Your neighbours called them nonsense, except on nights when the wind came down from the forest carrying a sound that was almost, but not quite, a voice.

On those nights, even the bravest among them barred their doors.

You had never seen anything in the woods. No pale figures between the trees, no strange lights drifting above the river, no eyes watching from the darkness. Whatever had happened in the ancient world, it had happened long before you were born.

And yet, sometimes, when you woke in the dead of night, you had the peculiar sensation that someone had just spoken your name.

Not aloud.

Not in a voice you could recognise.

As though something deep beneath the earth had remembered it.

You had never told anyone. There were enough reasons for people to think you strange without inventing new ones.

A gust of wind swept across the green, scattering dead leaves around your boots. You drew your clothing closer and turned towards the cottages. Smoke rose in straight columns from the chimneys, and the first stars had appeared above the rooftops. The village was settling into the comfortable hush of evening, its inhabitants retreating behind wooden doors and drawn curtains.

Somewhere, a child began to cry. Somewhere else, a couple argued over the price of grain. The ordinary machinery of life continued, indifferent to the dark gathering beyond the fields.

You should have gone inside.

Instead, you stood still and listened.

There it was again.

A sound from the forest.

Not an animal's call. Not the wind through the branches.

A single, low note, so deep that you felt it in your teeth before you understood that you were hearing it at all.

The conversation outside the alehouse faltered. The dog that had been barking fell silent. Across the green, the blacksmith emerged from his workshop, his heavy apron still tied around his waist, and stared towards the trees.

For one suspended heartbeat, the entire village seemed to hold its breath.

Then the sound vanished.

Someone laughed nervously. A door slammed. The blacksmith shook his head and returned to his forge, muttering about the weather. Within moments, the village began to move again, eager to bury the interruption beneath the familiar comforts of routine.

You tried to do the same.

But the unease beneath your ribs had changed. It was no longer the vague dissatisfaction of a life too small for its possibilities.

It was recognition.

You could not have explained what you recognised, or why the sound had made your hands go cold. You only knew that, for the first time in your life, the forest seemed less like a distant boundary and more like something standing on the other side of a door.

Something waiting.

You looked down at your hands. They were ordinary hands, reddened by the cold, with a thin scar across one knuckle and a smear of soot on your wrist. No strange markings. No unnatural light beneath your skin. Nothing to suggest that you were anything other than what you had always believed yourself to be.

You curled your fingers into your palms.

Whatever that sound had been, you would not let a childhood story make a fool of you.

There were still things to do before nightfall. People to see. A meal to find. A dozen small decisions that, taken together, would determine how the rest of your evening unfolded.

You turned towards the village.

Behind you, far beyond the last cottages, something moved between the trees.

And beneath your skin, something ancient stirred.

choices.text: Take a moment to yourself and breathe
Go and help with the evening tasks
Check the edges of the settlement, just to be sure
Seek out company or conversation

1.1b Early Village Connection.title: 1.2 Identity Choice – What You Are
1.1b Early Village Connection.text:
Morning arrived slowly in the valley, spilling pale gold across the rooftops and catching in the beads of dew that clung to the village green. A thin mist lingered over the river, curling between the reeds before lifting in delicate wisps towards the hills. Beyond the last cottages, the forest stood dark and watchful beneath the brightening sky, its upper branches stirring in a breeze that had not yet reached the village streets.

You stepped outside into the cool air and drew a deep breath. The scent of damp grass mingled with the comforting smell of fresh bread drifting from the bakery, where the ovens had been burning since before dawn. Somewhere nearby, a shutter banged open, followed by a woman's indignant muttering. A rooster crowed as though determined to announce the arrival of a new day personally.

You smiled despite yourself.

There was something reassuring about mornings here. No matter what troubles the world beyond the valley might be suffering, the village had its own steady rhythm. Fires needed lighting. Animals needed feeding. Bread needed baking. People needed one another, whether they cared to admit it or not.

"You're up early."

You turned to find Mara, the baker's wife, approaching with a basket balanced against her hip. A floury hand emerged from beneath her shawl to wave at you.

"Someone has to make certain you haven't burned the entire village down overnight," you replied.

She gasped in theatrical offence. "That happened once."

"Twice."

"The second time was the oven's fault."

"Of course it was."

Her laughter carried across the narrow lane, bright and unrestrained. She reached out to brush a stray fleck of something from your shoulder, the gesture so familiar that you barely noticed it.

"Here." She produced a small, still-warm roll from her basket and pressed it into your hand. "You look as though you forgot to eat yesterday."

"I ate."

"Something other than spite, I hope."

You laughed, and for a moment the morning seemed warmer.

Mara moved on towards the market square, already calling a greeting to someone further down the lane. You watched her go before breaking off a piece of bread. It was soft in the middle, with a crisp, golden crust, and the warmth seeped into your cold fingers.

You could not remember a time when Mara had not been part of your life. She had attended to scraped knees, soothed childhood fevers, and once chased a particularly persistent goose halfway across the village because it had stolen a ribbon from her daughter's hair. She knew everyone's business, claimed to know everyone's secrets, and had an alarming tendency to be right about both.

You would miss her terribly if you ever left.

The thought arrived uninvited, and you pushed it away.

By the time you reached the market square, the village was properly awake. Stalls were being assembled beneath faded awnings, and the cobbled ground rang with the clatter of wooden crates. A farmer unloaded sacks of grain from a cart while his youngest son attempted to persuade a particularly stubborn donkey to move. Two elderly women stood beside the well, deep in a discussion that had apparently begun the previous afternoon and showed no signs of reaching a conclusion.

"Morning!" called Tomas, the cooper, raising one broad hand from beside his stall.

You returned the greeting.

He was a mountain of a man, with a beard that had begun turning grey several years ago and shoulders that made the doorway of his workshop look suspiciously narrow. He had once attempted to teach you to roll a barrel down the main street without losing control of it. The barrel had survived. The fence had not.

Neither of you had ever quite forgiven the other for the incident.

"Any more plans to destroy my property?" he asked.

"Only if you leave it lying around."

"Cheeky wretch." He shook his head, but his smile betrayed him. "Your parents would be proud."

The words were spoken lightly, without malice, and yet something in you paused at them. Tomas seemed to notice. His expression softened, and he reached across the stall to squeeze your shoulder.

"Good to see you," he said simply.

"You too."

You meant it.

That was the strange thing about this place. Its people could be infuriating, nosy, stubborn, and occasionally impossible to reason with. They remembered every foolish thing you had ever done and were perfectly willing to remind you of it at the least convenient moment. They argued over fences, borrowed tools without returning them, and sometimes held grudges over matters so trivial that you could scarcely believe they were serious.

But they also left food on doorsteps when someone was ill. They repaired damaged roofs without being asked. When a family suffered a loss, the village gathered wood, prepared meals, and sat quietly beside them until the house no longer felt quite so empty.

No one needed to announce that these things mattered.

They simply did them.

You passed through the square, exchanging greetings as you went. A young mother caught your eye and lifted her baby so you could admire the child's newly acquired ability to grasp anything within reach. An old man sitting outside the meeting house nodded solemnly, then winked when he thought nobody was looking. A group of children scattered around your feet, laughing as they chased a hoop along the cobbles.

For a little while, you allowed yourself to belong without question.

The restlessness that had troubled you the previous evening seemed distant in the morning light. Here were the faces you knew, the voices that had shaped your childhood, the small rituals that made the passing seasons feel like chapters in a familiar story.

Whatever lay beyond the valley, this was your home.

And whatever the future might demand of you, you could not imagine a world in which these people meant nothing.

A bell rang from somewhere near the river, marking the hour. Around you, the square shifted from conversation to activity. Traders began calling their prices. Doors opened. Carts creaked towards the road.

The morning was moving on, and you had your own responsibilities waiting.

You finished the last of Mara's bread, brushed the crumbs from your hands, and turned towards the work that would occupy the rest of your day.

For now, there was nothing unusual about the morning.

For now, the world was still as it should be.

And you had no reason to suspect how little time remained before everything you knew would be reduced to ash.

choices.text: With the morning greetings finished, you turn your focus to your daily work

1.2 Identity Choice – What You Are.title: 1.2 Identity Choice – What You Are
1.2 Identity Choice – What You Are.text:
The morning passed into afternoon with the quiet inevitability of a river finding its course. The mist lifted from the valley, the sun climbed above the eastern hills, and the village settled into the steady business of living.

By midday, the market square had emptied of all but a handful of stubborn traders. Carts rattled along the lanes, carrying their goods towards neighbouring settlements, while the villagers returned to the tasks that could not be finished by conversation alone. Smoke rose from kitchen chimneys. Somewhere, a hammer struck iron in a steady rhythm. Beyond the cottages, cattle lowed in the fields, and the river flashed silver wherever the sunlight broke through the trees.

You moved through it all with the familiar ease of someone who belonged.

There were people who measured their lives in years, and others who measured them in journeys, fortunes, or victories. Here, life was measured in smaller things. The first frost. The harvest brought safely in. A child growing tall enough to reach the latch on the meeting-house door. A roof repaired before the rains. The return of a neighbour who had been away too long.

It was not an extraordinary existence, but it was a real one. Every person in the valley had a place in the intricate pattern of the village, whether they understood it or not. The farmer who coaxed grain from stubborn soil fed the baker. The blacksmith kept the farmer's tools working. The healer tended the injuries that came with both trades. Hunters brought meat from the forests when the fields could offer no more. Every skill mattered. Every pair of hands made the burden lighter for someone else.

You had never questioned that truth.

What you had questioned, occasionally and in the privacy of your own thoughts, was whether your own place in that pattern had been chosen for you or by you.

There was a difference, you suspected, though you had never quite worked out how to explain it.

The afternoon wore on. Shadows lengthened across the cobbles, stretching between the cottages like dark fingers. The last customers drifted away from the remaining stalls, and a chill crept into the air as the sun began its slow descent towards the western hills.

You found yourself glancing towards the village green.

A familiar figure crossed it carrying a bundle of firewood. Someone called your name from an open doorway, asking a question about tomorrow's weather. Two children argued over a wooden toy until an older sister intervened, confiscating it from both with the grim authority of a magistrate.

You smiled at the sight, but your attention kept returning to the tasks waiting beyond the square.

There was always something that needed doing. Something that someone had to take responsibility for, something that could not be left until tomorrow without making another person's life more difficult.

And, as much as you might sometimes wish otherwise, you had never been particularly good at pretending not to notice.

Perhaps that was why people trusted you. Perhaps it was simply because you had grown up among them, learning their habits and their troubles until the distinction between their needs and your own had become difficult to draw.

Whatever the reason, the village had shaped you as surely as the river had shaped the valley. Its people had taught you what mattered, its hardships had tested you, and its quiet kindnesses had given you reasons to stay.

Yet there was more than one way to serve a home.

Some people mended what was broken. Others made what was needed. Still others ventured beyond the safety of familiar walls, returning with the things no one else could provide.

You had spent years learning, consciously or otherwise, which of those paths felt most like your own.

Now the day was nearly done, and the work that remained belonged to you alone.

You paused at the junction where the main lane divided, one road leading towards the cottages clustered around the village well, another towards the workshops and their glowing hearths, and the last winding down towards the fields and the darkening forest beyond.

The evening breeze stirred the leaves at your feet.

You could hear the village behind you, its familiar sounds rising and falling in the gathering dusk. You knew these people. You knew what they needed. And whatever else the future might hold, you knew that the choices you made here would shape the person you became.

You turned towards the path that felt most like your own.

How had you chosen to make yourself useful in this world?

choices.text: I am the one they come to when the body fails – the healer
I shape things with my hands – wood, metal, or cloth – the craftsperson
I walk the wild edges and bring back what the village needs – the hunter

1.2b Family and Roots.title: 1.2b Family and Roots
1.2b Family and Roots.text:
By the time the sun began its descent behind the western hills, the village had settled into the familiar rhythm of evening. Shadows stretched across the cobblestones, long and bruised beneath the slate roofs, while smoke curled from chimneys into a sky slowly turning the colour of plums. Somewhere near the river, a cart rattled over uneven ground. A dog barked at its passing, and a woman called after a child who had evidently decided that supper could wait until one final game.

You knew these sounds as well as you knew your own heartbeat.

Whatever the day had demanded of you, whatever frustrations or small victories had filled its hours, the road home remained unchanged. It wound between the baker's cottage and the old well, past a crooked fence that had needed repairing since spring, and along a narrow lane where the houses grew fewer and the gardens gave way to untamed grass.

At the very edge of the settlement stood your cottage.

It was a modest place, built from grey stone quarried from the hills and roofed with slate darkened by decades of rain. Moss gathered between the stones near the foundations, and ivy climbed one wall despite your best efforts to keep it from swallowing the windows. The oak door had grown heavy with age, its iron hinges groaning whenever the weather turned damp. A small chimney leaned slightly to the east, and one shutter never quite closed properly.

It was not beautiful, at least not by the standards of the merchants who occasionally passed through the valley with their polished boots and expensive cloaks.

But it was yours.

Or, perhaps more accurately, it was the place to which you belonged.

You stopped outside the door for a moment, allowing the evening chill to settle against your skin. The cottage windows glowed with firelight, spilling narrow ribbons of gold across the threshold. Behind the walls, you could hear the faint sounds of domestic life: the scrape of a chair, the clink of a pot, the familiar murmur of a voice.

Someone was waiting for you.

The thought brought with it a complicated mixture of comfort and obligation. You had never been entirely certain where one ended and the other began. Love could make a burden easier to carry, but it could also make setting it down feel like betrayal. Duty might keep a roof above someone's head, yet it had a habit of creeping into every corner of a life until there was little room left for anything else.

You understood that better than most.

There were days when you imagined what it might be like to walk beyond the valley without looking back. To travel the old roads, see the cities whose names appeared on merchants' maps, and discover whether the world was truly as dangerous as the village elders insisted. You wondered what it would feel like to make a choice based entirely on your own desires.

Then you would think of the people inside your cottage, and the imagined journey would become more complicated.

The village had taught you that lives were rarely lived in isolation. People depended upon one another, sometimes willingly, sometimes because circumstances had left them no other choice. Families shared food when harvests failed. Neighbours repaired roofs after storms. The sick were tended, the grieving were accompanied, and the lonely were occasionally dragged to supper whether they wished to attend or not.

These were small acts, easily overlooked by anyone searching for grand displays of courage or devotion.

Yet they were the things that kept a place alive.

You lifted your hand towards the door, then hesitated.

The last light caught the iron ring beneath your fingers. Beyond the village, the forest had already begun to darken, its branches merging into a single jagged silhouette against the sky. You remembered the strange sound from the previous evening, the deep note that had silenced the village for one impossible heartbeat.

You had heard nothing since.

Perhaps it had been an animal. Perhaps the wind had carried some unfamiliar sound down from the mountains. There were a hundred sensible explanations, and you had no intention of surrendering to superstition merely because the woods looked unsettling after sunset.

Still, you found yourself listening before entering.

Nothing.

Only the breeze moving through the grass, the distant call of a night bird, and the gentle crackle of a fire burning behind the walls.

You pushed open the door.

Warmth met you first, followed by the scent of woodsmoke and whatever had been left to simmer near the hearth. The main room was much as you remembered it: a scarred wooden table, two or three chairs that did not quite match, shelves crowded with practical necessities, and a collection of small possessions that had accumulated over years of living. A woollen blanket lay folded across the settle. A chipped bowl rested beside the washbasin. Above the fireplace, a handful of dried flowers had been tied together with string and left to fade.

Nothing here would have impressed a passing noble.

Everything here mattered.

You stepped over the threshold and closed the heavy door behind you. For a moment, you remained with your hand resting against the oak, allowing the familiar quiet to settle around you.

Whatever the outside world might demand, whatever secrets lay buried beneath the valley's ancient roots, your life had been shaped by the people who shared this place with you.

And now, as evening gathered beyond the windows, you were about to remember precisely what that meant.

When you step inside through the heavy oak door at the end of a hard day, who shares this hearth with you?

choices.text: Your aging parents, whose slow cough and tired bones anchor you to this roof.
Your younger sibling, whose restless energy and constant questions remind you why you work.
No one. You live alone in the quiet dark, answering only to yourself.

1.2c Afternoon Transition.title: 1.2c Afternoon Transition
1.2c Afternoon Transition.text:
The cottage welcomed you with its familiar warmth, but the comfort of home was a brief reprieve rather than an end to the day's responsibilities.

Outside, the last of the afternoon light slipped from the rooftops, leaving the village lanes in shadow. A chill crept up from the river, carrying the scent of damp leaves and woodsmoke. One by one, the windows of the neighbouring cottages brightened as lamps were lit and families gathered around their evening meals.

You had always liked this hour, though you rarely had the luxury of enjoying it for long. There was something honest about the village at dusk. The day's work was nearly done, its successes and failures already becoming tomorrow's problems. People were tired, tempers occasionally frayed, and the ordinary business of keeping one another alive continued regardless.

You understood that better than most.

Your homecoming, however, depended upon who was waiting inside.

<<if $familyOrigin is "parents">
For those whose aging parents shared the cottage, the first moments belonged to quiet acts of care. You checked that they were comfortable, listened for the familiar rhythm of their breathing, and made certain the hearth had enough wood to last through the night. Perhaps one of them protested that you fussed too much. Perhaps the other asked whether you had eaten, despite the fact that they had been asking the same question for years. Their bodies might be growing frail, but their determination to remain useful had not diminished. You knew the day would come when their chairs stood empty beside the fire. For now, you treasured the ordinary inconvenience of having to look after them.

<<elseif $familyOrigin is "younger_sibling">
For those living with a younger sibling, home offered a different sort of chaos. A crust of bread tossed across the room might earn a delighted grin, followed by a question that had been waiting impatiently all afternoon. Your sibling had an inexhaustible supply of curiosity and an apparent inability to recognise when an adult had no time to answer. There were moments when the responsibility felt exhausting. There were others when their laughter made the burdens of the day seem smaller. You might grumble, but you would always make certain there was enough food, enough warmth, and enough safety for them to grow up believing the world could be a good place.

<<else>>
And for those who lived alone, the cottage offered something rarer: silence without obligation. You could bolt the heavy timber door, set down your belongings, and enjoy the stillness without needing to explain yourself to anyone. There was comfort in that independence, in the freedom to arrange your evenings according to your own wishes. Yet solitude had its own peculiar weight. Sometimes the quiet was a welcome companion; sometimes it reminded you that there was no one to notice if you failed to return.

<</if>>
Whichever life you led, the cottage remained a place to gather yourself before stepping back into the world.

You took a moment to settle your belongings, straighten what needed straightening, and prepare for the hours ahead. Perhaps you glanced at the fading light through the window. Perhaps you paused beside the hearth, allowing the warmth to loosen the stiffness in your shoulders. The day's work had left its marks on you, whether in tired muscles, stained hands, or the lingering strain of decisions made under pressure.

But the village had not finished asking things of you.

Somewhere beyond your door, a neighbour might be waiting for help. A task might have gone unfinished. Someone might be hungry, injured, or in need of something that only you could provide. Your trade was not merely a way to earn your place in the community. It was one of the threads binding your life to everyone else's.

You drew a final breath of warm cottage air and turned towards the evening.

The sun was nearly gone. Soon, the valley would belong to the dark.

There was still work to do.

choices.text: Your aging parents, whose slow cough and tired bones anchor you to this roof.
Your younger sibling, whose restless energy and constant questions remind you why you work.
No one. You live alone in the quiet dark, answering only to yourself.

1.3a Healer’s Late Afternoon.title: 1.3a Healer’s Late Afternoon
1.3a Healer’s Late Afternoon.text:
The first knock came before you had finished washing the day's work from your hands.

Three sharp raps against the cottage door, followed by a woman's voice calling your name with the particular urgency of someone who had already decided that waiting was unacceptable.

You dried your fingers on a linen cloth and crossed the room.

"What's happened?"

"It's little Elsie," said Mara, the baker's wife. Her cheeks were flushed from the cold, and loose strands of hair clung to her forehead. "She's burning up. Her mother says she's been poorly since midday, and now she won't wake properly."

You reached for your satchel.

"How long has she had the fever?"

"Since this morning, perhaps. Her mother thought it was a chill."

You did not waste time asking why they had waited. Fear made people hopeful, and hope often persuaded them that a child would recover if they simply kept the blankets warm and the prayers coming.

You followed Mara through the gathering dusk, your satchel knocking against your hip. The village lanes had grown muddy after the previous night's rain, and you stepped carefully around the deepest ruts. Smoke drifted low between the cottages, stinging your eyes. Somewhere nearby, a pot clattered to the ground, followed by a muffled curse.

Ordinary sounds. Ordinary troubles.

You repeated the thought to yourself as you hurried along.

The healer's work was rarely dramatic. It was a succession of small judgements, made with incomplete information and the uncomfortable knowledge that being wrong could cost someone dearly. You knew which herbs eased a cough, which poultices helped draw infection from a wound, and how to recognise the dangerous stillness that sometimes followed a prolonged fever. You had learned to listen before speaking, to ask questions that frightened people might forget to answer, and never to promise a recovery simply because someone desperately needed to hear one.

Still, there were nights when knowledge felt painfully small.

Elsie's family lived in a low cottage near the village well. When you entered, the heat struck you first, thick with the smell of damp wool and boiled water. Her mother sat beside the bed, twisting a handkerchief between her fingers. The child lay beneath a pile of blankets, her cheeks unnaturally red, her breathing shallow and uneven.

You set your satchel on the table.

"How much has she had to drink?"

"Some water. A little broth, but she wouldn't take any more."

"And has she been sick?"

"Twice."

You knelt beside the bed and touched the back of your fingers to Elsie's forehead. The heat was alarming. You gently lifted one of her eyelids, watched her response, and checked her breathing before placing two fingers against the inside of her wrist.

Her pulse fluttered beneath your fingertips.

Too fast. Too weak.

You swallowed your concern and examined her more carefully, asking her mother about the morning, the previous evening, and anyone else in the household who had been unwell. You checked for a rash, looked for signs of dehydration, and listened to her chest as best you could in the crowded room.

You had seen children recover from worse.

You had also seen children fail to recover from less.

"Fetch me a clean bowl and some cool water," you said. "And remove the extra blankets. She needs to be comfortable, not smothered."

Her mother hesitated.

"But she's shivering."

"I know. We'll keep her warm enough without trapping all that heat."

The woman obeyed, though her hands shook as she worked.

You prepared a simple infusion from your supplies, choosing the ingredients with care. You had no miracle cure hidden among your jars, no secret knowledge that could command a body to mend itself. There were only the remedies you understood, the symptoms you could interpret, and the patient attention that sometimes made the difference between a manageable illness and a dangerous one.

As you worked, you spoke quietly to Elsie, even though she was too drowsy to answer. You told her that her mother was nearby. You told her that the water would feel cool against her skin. You reminded her of the wooden horse she had shown you the previous week, its painted mane crooked and one wheel missing.

"Though I suspect," you murmured, "that horse is in better condition than most of the men who come to me complaining about their backs."

A faint sound escaped Elsie's mother. Not quite a laugh, but close enough.

It was a small thing. You counted it as a victory.

Time passed in a blur of cool cloths, careful observation, and quiet instructions. Outside, the light drained from the windows. You asked a neighbour to fetch additional water and made certain someone remained with the child. When Elsie's breathing grew more settled, you allowed yourself to release a fraction of the tension in your shoulders.

Then her pulse stumbled.

Your fingers froze against her wrist.

For one unsettling instant, the beat beneath your fingertips seemed to stop altogether. Not weaken. Not falter. Stop.

You leaned closer, your attention narrowing until the sounds of the cottage disappeared beneath the rush of blood in your ears.

There.

A beat.

Another.

Her pulse resumed, rapid but regular enough to reassure you that she was still responding.

You exhaled slowly.

Exhaustion, you decided. You had been working since early morning, and the cold had settled into your joints. Fingers slipped. Pulses could be difficult to find in a feverish child.

There was no reason to invent something extraordinary when an ordinary explanation would suffice.

Then came the smell.

Faint and fleeting, it drifted through the air above the bed: dry woodsmoke, bitter and old, like the remains of a fire that had burned long after everyone had abandoned the hearth.

You lifted your head.

The fire in the corner had burned low. No one had added wood for some time, and its embers glowed beneath a thin layer of ash. Perhaps a draught had stirred the remains. Perhaps you had simply noticed the smell because you were tired.

You glanced towards the hearth, then back at Elsie.

Her breathing had eased. The fever had begun to break, leaving a sheen of sweat along her temples. Her mother covered her mouth with both hands, tears gathering in her eyes.

"Is she going to be all right?"

You considered your answer before giving it.

"She's improved. That's encouraging, but I want someone watching her closely through the night. If her breathing worsens, if she becomes harder to wake, or if anything changes suddenly, send for me immediately."

The woman's expression crumpled with relief. She caught your hand and pressed it between both of hers.

"Thank you."

You nodded, uncomfortable with the gratitude. You had done what you could. That was all anyone could honestly promise.

When you finally packed your satchel, Elsie was sleeping more peacefully, her mother sitting beside her with one hand resting against the child's hair.

You stepped outside into the cold.

The village had grown quiet. Lamps glowed behind shuttered windows, and the first stars had appeared above the rooftops. You stood on the doorstep for a moment, flexing your aching fingers.

The smell of ash lingered faintly in your memory.

You told yourself it meant nothing.

You had patients to check on tomorrow, herbs to replenish, and a dozen ordinary problems waiting to be solved. The world was difficult enough without searching for mysteries in every shadow.

So you turned towards home.

Behind you, in the cottage where the child slept, the fire gave a sudden, soundless flicker.

Every ember burned white for the space of a single heartbeat.

Then the hearth settled into darkness.

choices.text: Continue into the evening

1.3b Craftsperson’s Late Afternoon.title: 1.3b Craftsperson’s Late Afternoon
1.3b Craftsperson’s Late Afternoon.text:
The commission was supposed to have been finished by midday.

You had made that promise three days ago, when the merchant arrived at your workshop with a purse of silver, an impatient expression, and a wooden chest that he claimed had belonged to his grandmother. The chest was meant to be a wedding gift for his eldest daughter, and he wanted its broken hinges replaced, its warped lid repaired, and its surface polished until it shone like new.

A simple enough job.

Unfortunately, the merchant's grandmother had apparently possessed a remarkable talent for breaking things in ways that made them difficult to mend.

You leaned over the workbench, examining the troublesome lid beneath the warm glow of your oil lamp. Shavings of pale wood littered the floor around your boots. Your fingers ached from hours of careful work, and a dark smear of grease marked the sleeve of your shirt. Outside, the last of the afternoon light was fading behind the rooftops, but the workshop remained warm from the small brazier burning beside the forge.

You had always preferred working into the evening. There were fewer interruptions, fewer customers leaning over your shoulder to offer suggestions, and fewer people asking whether something would be finished soon.

The irony of this particular commission was not lost on you.

You adjusted the chest beneath the lamp and ran your fingertips along the repaired edge. The wood was old oak, darkened by years of handling, with a tight grain that had resisted your tools throughout the afternoon. You had replaced the worst of the damaged timber and fitted a new hinge, but the lid still refused to sit quite flush against the frame.

You could have forced it.

A lesser craftsperson might have done so, hidden the gap beneath a decorative strip, and collected the payment without another thought.

You found the idea offensive.

Wood had its own character. It expanded and contracted with the seasons, twisted when it dried, and occasionally split simply because some forgotten knot had decided to make your life difficult. Metal behaved differently, but it too had its stubborn moments. Every material demanded that you understand it before you could persuade it to become something useful.

You had learned that lesson the hard way, through burned fingers, broken tools, and several expensive mistakes that you preferred not to remember.

You set down your chisel and reached for a narrow plane.

"Come on," you muttered to the chest. "We're both too old for this nonsense."

The tool slid across the wood, shaving away a thin curl. You adjusted the angle and tried again.

This time, the lid settled into place with a satisfying click.

You sat back, allowing yourself a small smile.

There. A little patience, a little precision, and a willingness to admit when your first approach had been wrong. Most problems could be solved with those three things, provided you had enough time and the necessary materials.

People were rather less predictable.

You had spent enough hours repairing broken furniture to recognise that damage rarely announced itself honestly. A crack might begin beneath the surface, invisible until the weight became too great. A joint could look sound while the smallest movement threatened to pull it apart. The most beautiful pieces were not necessarily the strongest, and the most damaged could sometimes be restored with a little care.

Perhaps that was why you liked your work.

Things made sense when you understood how they fitted together.

You reached for the small brass hinge lying beside the chest and held it up to the lamplight. It caught a thin ribbon of gold across its surface. You turned it between your fingers, checking the pin and the alignment, then reached for your hammer.

The moment your hand closed around its handle, the tool began to hum.

You froze.

It was a faint vibration, barely more than a tremor travelling through the wood and into your palm. Yet you felt it distinctly, a low, steady note that seemed to rise from somewhere deep inside the hammer's iron head.

Your fingers tightened.

The vibration stopped.

You stared at the tool.

The workshop was quiet except for the faint crackle of the brazier and the wind pressing against the shutters. You lifted the hammer, turned it over, and inspected the head for a loose fitting or a crack in the handle.

Nothing.

You tapped it against the workbench.

A perfectly ordinary sound answered you.

You frowned, then gave a short, humourless laugh.

"Too many hours."

You had been working since dawn. Your hands were tired, your eyes strained, and the oil lamp had begun to smoke. There were a dozen sensible reasons for an odd sensation, and none of them required you to believe that your tools had developed opinions.

You returned to the chest.

The next hinge fitted without difficulty. You tightened the screws, tested the lid, and opened and closed it several times. The movement was smooth, the repaired wood sitting neatly against the frame.

Satisfied, you reached for a cloth and began rubbing the surface with oil.

As the finish darkened, the grain emerged in delicate patterns beneath your hands. Fine lines curled through the oak, branching and reconnecting in shapes that reminded you of river channels on an old map. You followed one with your eyes, watching it disappear beneath a darker knot near the corner.

For an instant, the reflection of your hand in the polished surface moved a heartbeat too late.

You stopped rubbing.

The reflected fingers continued their movement, dragging the cloth another inch across the wood before coming to rest.

Your own hand remained perfectly still.

The silence that followed seemed enormous.

You bent closer to the chest, your heart giving an uncomfortable thud against your ribs. The reflection was ordinary now, broken only by the wavering light of the oil lamp. You shifted your hand from side to side, testing the surface, searching for some trick of the grain or the angle of the light.

Nothing happened.

A draught, you decided. A flicker of flame. Tired eyes.

You had no intention of letting an expensive piece of furniture become the subject of a village ghost story.

You finished polishing the chest, wrapped it carefully in linen, and placed it beside the door for collection in the morning. Then you extinguished the lamp and began clearing the shavings from your workbench.

Your shoulders protested when you straightened. Your fingers were stiff, and the small ache behind your eyes had settled into something more persistent.

Outside, the village had surrendered to night. Warm squares of light glowed through the cottage windows, and somewhere along the lane a familiar voice called goodnight to a neighbour.

You listened for a moment, comforted by the ordinary sounds.

Whatever strange impressions had troubled you during the evening, they had passed. The hammer was only a hammer. The chest was only a chest. Wood warped, lamps flickered, and tired people occasionally imagined things they could not explain.

You had spent your life learning how to make sense of the material world.

You would not abandon that knowledge because of a few inexplicable moments.

Still, as you reached for the workshop door, you glanced back at the covered chest.

Beneath the linen, something gave a soft, single knock.

You stood motionless.

Then the brazier settled with a crack, and the sound was gone.

You locked the door and stepped into the cold evening air.

There was work to be done tomorrow.

For now, that was enough.

choices.text: Continue into the evening

1.3c Hunter’s Late Afternoon.title: 1.3c Hunter’s Late Afternoon
1.3c Hunter’s Late Afternoon.text:
The forest was supposed to be empty at this hour.

You had spent most of the afternoon following the narrow paths that wound through the hills beyond the village, checking snares, searching for fresh tracks, and watching the places where deer sometimes came down to drink. The autumn woods had grown stingy in recent weeks. The rabbits were harder to find, the squirrels had retreated into the higher branches, and the larger game seemed to have moved deeper into the hills ahead of the winter cold.

You had still managed to secure a hare and two pheasants, enough to justify the walk and contribute something useful to the village stores. It was not a spectacular haul, but you had never expected the forest to provide generously every day.

The woods demanded patience. They rewarded those who paid attention and punished those who assumed they knew too much.

You had learned that lesson long before you were trusted to hunt beyond the settlement alone.

Now, with the sun sinking towards the western ridge, you crouched beside the last of your snares and brushed a scatter of damp leaves away from the trigger. The cord was intact. The small wooden peg remained in place. Nothing had disturbed it.

You reset the mechanism carefully, testing the tension with your thumb before covering it again.

A hunter's work was not merely the act of killing. It was knowing where an animal might travel, recognising the difference between a fresh track and one softened by rain, and understanding when to leave a place undisturbed. Every careless step left evidence. Every broken branch told a story. The forest was full of information, provided you were willing to read it.

You rose, shouldered your bow, and began the walk home.

The path descended through a stand of ancient oaks, their broad trunks furred with moss. Their leaves had turned the colour of old copper, and the ground beneath them was thick with damp foliage. Shafts of sunlight filtered through the canopy, illuminating drifting motes of dust and the occasional spiderweb strung between branches.

You knew this stretch of woodland well.

You knew the hollow where foxes denned, the fallen tree that concealed a narrow stream, and the patch of brambles where you had once lost an entire afternoon extracting a rabbit from a particularly unfortunate tangle. You knew which roots would trip an unwary traveller and which branches would crack beneath a careless foot.

You also knew the sounds.

A woodpecker tapping somewhere to the north. The rustle of a squirrel crossing a branch. The faint rush of water beyond the slope. The occasional distant call of a bird announcing its territory to rivals you would never see.

You moved through them quietly, letting the forest reveal itself at its own pace.

Then you noticed the deer.

It stood between two trees ahead of you, half concealed by the undergrowth. A young stag, lean from the season, its coat darkened by the damp. Its antlers were still modest, little more than branching points above its head.

You stopped.

The animal had not heard you approach. You were certain of it. The wind was carrying your scent away from the clearing, and your boots had made scarcely a sound against the soft ground.

Yet the stag was looking directly at you.

You waited for it to bolt.

Wild animals were rarely comfortable with a human's gaze. Even those accustomed to the distant presence of hunters usually fled once they realised they had been seen. This one remained perfectly still, its ears forward, its dark eyes fixed on your face.

You lowered your bow hand.

"Go on," you murmured.

The stag did not move.

A faint crease formed between your brows. You had seen curious animals before, but there was something unsettling about the way it watched you. It did not seem frightened. Nor did it appear to be assessing whether you posed a threat.

It looked as though it recognised you.

The thought was absurd. You had never seen this particular animal before, and even if you had, a deer would hardly remember a passing hunter with such peculiar intensity.

You shifted your weight.

The stag tilted its head.

For a brief, uncomfortable instant, you had the impression that it was waiting for you to say something.

A gust of wind stirred the leaves overhead. The branches swayed, and the stag turned its head towards the sound. When you looked back at it, the animal had stepped into the undergrowth and vanished between the trees.

You exhaled.

There was nothing remarkable about that. Deer were quick, and the forest offered countless places to hide. You had simply been caught staring.

You continued down the path.

A little farther on, the ground grew softer beside the stream. You slowed automatically, scanning the mud for tracks. A fox had passed through recently, leaving a neat line of prints between the exposed roots. Beyond them, larger impressions marked the earth: a hoofprint, then another, followed by the unmistakable split shape of a deer's track.

You crouched to examine them.

Fresh. Very fresh.

The prints led towards the stream, where the mud darkened beneath the overhanging branches. You followed them with your eyes, tracing their path around a moss-covered stone and towards a narrow gap between two trees.

Then they stopped.

Not faded. Not obscured by leaves or broken ground.

Stopped.

The final hoofprints lay in a patch of wet earth barely three paces from the stone. Beyond them, the ground was smooth and undisturbed. There were no marks suggesting a leap, no scuffs where the animal might have scrambled up the slope, no evidence that it had doubled back.

You stared at the empty ground.

You had tracked animals through snow, rain, and terrain so rocky that even an experienced hunter might struggle to distinguish one footprint from another. You knew how easily a trail could become confusing.

But this was not confusion.

It was an absence.

You stood slowly and looked into the trees.

The forest had gone silent.

The stream still flowed, but its sound seemed strangely distant. The birds had stopped calling. Even the leaves above you had ceased their restless movement, though the air against your face remained cold.

You became acutely aware of your own breathing.

Something about the silence felt deliberate, as though the woodland had noticed you and was waiting to see what you would do.

Your fingers tightened around the strap of your hunting bag.

You listened.

One heartbeat. Two.

Then a branch cracked somewhere behind you.

You turned sharply, bow half raised.

Nothing stood between the trees. No movement disturbed the undergrowth. The path behind you was empty, winding back towards the village beneath the darkening canopy.

The ordinary sounds of the forest returned all at once. A bird called from the northern slope. Water rushed over the stones. Leaves stirred in the breeze.

You lowered your bow.

"Tired," you muttered, though the word sounded unconvincing even to your own ears.

You had been in the woods since morning. You were hungry, cold, and eager to reach the village before darkness made the path difficult to navigate. There were sensible explanations for everything you had seen.

You gathered your bag more securely and resumed your journey.

By the time you reached the edge of the settlement, the first lamps were burning behind the cottage windows. The smell of woodsmoke drifted across the fields, and the familiar outline of the rooftops emerged against the violet sky.

You glanced back once.

The forest stood as it always had: ancient, dark, and indifferent.

You turned towards home.

Behind you, deep beneath the trees, something moved without disturbing a single leaf.

And somewhere along the path you had just travelled, a fresh set of hoofprints appeared in the damp earth.

They followed your tracks towards the village.

choices.text: Continue into the evening

1.4 First Home LI Interaction.title: 1.4 First Home LI Interaction
1.4 First Home LI Interaction.text:
By dusk, the cottage has settled into the familiar quiet of evening.

Outside, the last light drains from the sky, leaving the fields beyond the northern edge of the village a deep, colourless grey. The wind has risen since afternoon, slipping beneath the eaves and worrying at the shutters. Somewhere beyond the gardens, a dog barks twice before falling silent. The smell of damp earth and woodsmoke seeps through the cracks around the door.

Inside, the hearth throws a low amber glow across the stone walls. Shadows gather in the corners, softening the uneven edges of the furniture and making the old cottage seem smaller, warmer, more removed from the world beyond its door.

<<if $familyOrigin is "parents">
In the back room, your parents are settled for the night. You heard the familiar creak of your mother's bed a little while ago, followed by your father's quiet murmur as he banked the fire in their hearth. Their presence is reassuring, even when you cannot see them. The main room belongs to you now, its quiet interrupted only by the occasional shift of settling timber.>

<<elseif $familyOrigin is "younger_sibling">
Your younger sibling has finally drifted off on the rug beside the fire, exhaustion overcoming whatever stubborn determination had kept them awake. One arm is folded beneath their head, and the blanket you placed over their shoulders has slipped halfway to the floor. You pause to pull it back into place. For a moment, you let yourself simply watch them breathe, grateful for the ordinary peace of it.>

<<else>>
The cottage is silent, save for the crackle of dry pine in the grate. Without another person moving through the rooms, every little sound seems sharper: the wind against the shutters, the faint tick of cooling iron, the soft creak of the old floorboards beneath your feet. You have grown accustomed to solitude, but tonight the quiet feels unusually attentive.>
<</if>>

A knock sounds at the door.

You know who it is before you reach the latch.

Kael never knocks as though he expects to be turned away. Three solid raps, a pause, and then the scrape of his boot against the threshold, as if he has already decided you are taking too long.

When you open the door, a gust of cold air follows him inside.

He stands broad-shouldered against the fading light, his dark cloak damp at the edges and carrying the sharp scent of the outdoors. A bundle of split logs rests against one arm, with kindling tucked beneath the other. His hair has been ruffled by the wind, and a stray leaf clings to the shoulder of his cloak.

“You were going to run out of wood,” he says by way of greeting.

You look past him towards the neatly stacked pile beside the door. “I have wood.”

“You have three logs and a collection of sticks that would struggle to light a candle.”

“They are perfectly good sticks.”

“They are damp.”

“They are nearly dry.”

Kael gives you a look that has changed very little since childhood. It once accompanied scraped knees, broken fences, and the occasional disastrous attempt to climb the old apple tree near the meeting house. It means he has heard your argument, found it unconvincing, and intends to proceed regardless.

He steps inside.

“Move,” he says, nudging you aside with his shoulder. “Before you freeze to death defending your sticks.”

You shut the door behind him, trying not to smile.

There is something deeply familiar about watching Kael settle into a room. He knows which floorboard complains beneath his weight, which hook will hold his cloak, and where you keep the iron poker. He has been crossing this threshold for so many years that his presence seems less like a visitor's and more like another piece of the cottage itself.

He drops the logs beside the hearth and kneels to arrange them, broad hands working with unhurried confidence. The cold clings to him as he moves, bringing the scent of pine, rain, and the forest's dark soil into the room.

“You look pale,” he says.

You glance down at yourself. “An extraordinary observation.”

“I'm serious.”

“So am I. You should consider making a living as a healer.”

His expression does not change. “What happened this afternoon?”

The question catches you off guard. You had thought the day's unease was hidden beneath the usual irritations and small tasks, tucked away where nobody would think to look.

“Nothing happened.”

“That's not an answer.”

“It is an answer. You simply dislike it.”

Kael straightens, brushing a smear of ash from his fingers. His gaze searches your face, not quite suspicious, but too familiar to be fooled by your deflection.

“I saw people coming back from the green,” he says. “They were talking about the sound.”

The room seems to contract around the words.

You remember it: that deep, distant note rising from beyond the trees, too low to be thunder and too long to be any ordinary animal's cry. It had travelled through the ground as much as through the air. For one strange instant, you had felt it beneath your ribs, as though something buried far below the village had stirred and drawn breath.

You had told yourself it was the wind.

Everyone else seemed to have found their own explanation.

“What did you hear?” you ask.

Kael looks towards the shuttered window.

“Enough to know it wasn't thunder.”

For once, there is no teasing in his voice.

He feeds another piece of kindling into the hearth. The flame catches, briefly illuminating the tired lines around his eyes. You wonder how much of the day's strangeness he has been carrying alone, and whether he came here because he was worried about you or because he did not want to sit with it himself.

“People are frightened,” you say.

“People are always frightened when they can't name something.”

“And you?”

He considers the question.

“I am frightened when something happens and everyone decides not to talk about it.”

You look at him then, properly. Kael has never been particularly skilled at pretending not to care. He hides concern behind practical tasks, sharp remarks, and the assumption that if he can mend something, carry it, or stand between it and trouble, the problem might be made smaller.

He has done it for you since you were children.

You remember him standing beside you after the riverbank fall, insisting your scraped palms needed washing while you insisted you were perfectly fine. You remember the two of you sharing stolen pastries beneath the apple tree, both pretending not to notice that he had given you the larger half. You remember years of arguments, silences, and reconciliations so ordinary that neither of you ever thought to name what held you together.

Now he sits beside you on the hearthstone, close enough that your shoulders nearly touch.

“You don't have to carry everything yourself,” he says quietly.

The words are familiar. They should be easy to dismiss.

Instead, you find yourself looking at the fire because looking at him feels suddenly more difficult.

“And you don't have to bring me firewood every time you think I'm troubled.”

“I know.”

“You could simply ask.”

“I just did.”

You let out a reluctant laugh. Kael's mouth curves at the sound, and for a few moments the cottage feels like itself again: warm, safe, full of things that have always been true.

Then a knock sounds at the wooden latch.

Two quick taps. A pause. Then a third.

You and Kael both turn towards the door.

The rhythm is familiar. It is the knock people use when they need help and do not want to shout the reason into the street.

A voice comes from the other side, strained by cold and urgency.

“Please. I need someone.”

Kael rises, his expression sharpening. He glances at you, and the unspoken question between you is as old as your friendship: Are you going?

Beyond the door, the visitor knocks again.

The hearth crackles behind you. Outside, the village has gone very quiet.
